title: A new hepatitis C result
note: Fictional patient and unit. The steps follow the module’s cited guidelines; your unit’s licensing requirements, written policy, infection control team and the attending nephrologist come first.
intro:
You are the nephrology fellow on the dialysis rotation of a hospital hemodialysis (HD) unit in Bacolod City. The unit screens every in-center patient for hepatitis C virus (HCV) every 6 months, as the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) 2022 guideline recommends (1B).

This round, one result is new. Mr. Rodel Villanueva, 47, a jeepney driver who has dialyzed through a fistula for three years, tested negative six months ago and is now positive on immunoassay. He has had no transfusion or surgery since then; he had a dental cleaning three months ago. He dialyzes on the second shift at station 6. The unit’s written policy, under its Department of Health (DOH) license, assigns HCV-positive patients to a separate area with dedicated machines. The attending nephrologist is also the medical director.

choices.text: Note the dental cleaning as the likely source, and recheck him at the next 6-month screening.
choices.feedback: A new positive in a previously negative patient is unit-acquired transmission until shown otherwise. KDIGO recommends that centers examine and track every HCV result (1B). Six months of waiting exposes every shift.
choices.then: The infection control nurse sees the result on the laboratory list and calls you. You bring it to the attending.

choices.text: Tell the attending today, confirm it, treat it as possibly acquired here, notify infection control.
choices.feedback: KDIGO asks centers to track every result (1B). The module’s cluster table lists a new hepatitis C result in a previously negative patient as a stop-and-call event, because the next shift is already exposed. Start reviewing every patient’s results.

choices.text: Move him quietly into the HCV area and tell no one, so the other patients do not panic.
choices.feedback: Silence leaves the source in place. If transmission happened in the unit, hands, vials and carts keep spreading it while the index patient sits elsewhere.
choices.then: The head nurse asks why he was moved. You take the result to the attending and infection control.

choices.text: Wait for the confirmatory test before telling anyone, so no one is alarmed by a false positive.
choices.feedback: Confirming is right, but telling the attending and infection control should not wait for it. The review can start while the confirmation runs.
choices.then: The confirmation comes back positive two days later. You inform the attending and infection control.

n2.prompt: Infection control asks what the review should cover. What do you propose?

choices.text: Test the patients on the chairs on either side of station 6, since spread is usually local.
choices.feedback: Neighbors matter, but transmission follows hands, gloves, shared vials and supply carts across the whole room, not only the chairs beside him.
choices.then: The infection control nurse asks for a full line list instead.

vitals.review: Line list: results, stations, shifts, staff, vials

choices.text: Stop dialyzer reuse for everyone, because reprocessing must be the source.
choices.feedback: KDIGO suggests that dialyzers can be reused if standard procedures are followed (2D). The reuse procedure belongs in the audit, but jumping to it skips the review of technique that the evidence points to.
choices.then: The attending asks for the full review first. You build the line list.

vitals.review: Line list: results, stations, shifts, staff, vials

choices.text: A line list of results, stations and shifts, medicine preparation, and direct observation.
choices.feedback: The module’s first checks for a new hepatitis result are all results, station and staff assignments, vial use, and enhanced audits. The pattern across patients points to the route. Every patient’s HCV results, his station, machine and shift, the patients and staff around him, how medicines are prepared and which vials are shared; observe hand hygiene, injection safety and cleaning.

vitals.review: Line list: results, stations, shifts, staff, vials

n3.scene: You watch the second shift. A nurse draws heparin flushes from one multidose vial on a cart parked between stations 5 and 6, then moves from station 6 to station 7 without changing gloves or cleaning her hands.
n3.prompt: What do you recommend to the medical director?

choices.text: Nothing new: once Mr. Villanueva moves to the HCV area, the problem is contained.
choices.feedback: The lapse you watched affects every patient on the shift. A separate area can create a false sense of safety while hands and vials keep spreading the virus.
choices.then: The infection control nurse shows the attending your observation notes. The unit starts the measures anyway.

vitals.audit: Retraining done; monthly observation with feedback

choices.text: Aggressive measures: hand hygiene, clean medicine preparation, no shared vials, monthly audits.
choices.feedback: When a new infection is likely unit-acquired, KDIGO recommends aggressive measures to improve hand hygiene, injection safety and environmental cleaning (1A), with regular observational audits (1C). The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) list monthly hand hygiene observations with feedback among their core interventions. New gloves at every station, medicines prepared away from the chairs, no vial or cart between stations, cleaning of each station zone, monthly observations with feedback.

vitals.audit: Retraining done; monthly observation with feedback

choices.text: Send a memo reminding all staff to change gloves between patients, and post it at each station.
choices.feedback: The content is right, but a memo without observation and feedback rarely changes what happens at the chair, and it leaves the shared vial and cart untouched.
choices.then: The medical director turns the memo into retraining with monthly observed audits.

vitals.audit: Retraining done; monthly observation with feedback

n4.scene: The head nurse asks you: “Our written policy says he goes to the HCV area with a dedicated machine. Do we move him?”

choices.text: Follow the policy for now, say isolation does not replace clean hands, and ask for a review.
choices.feedback: KDIGO recommends against dedicated machines (1D, low certainty) and suggests against isolation (2C), because transmission tracks breaks in technique. A unit still follows its licensing rules; the place to change a policy is the medical director’s review, not the chair. Bring KDIGO 2022 to the medical director for a policy review.

choices.text: No. KDIGO recommends against dedicated machines, so ignore the unit’s policy and keep him at station 6.
choices.feedback: The KDIGO grade is 1D, low certainty, and the unit operates under its DOH license and written policy. Overriding it at the chair is not your call; take the evidence to the medical director.
choices.then: The head nurse checks with the medical director, who keeps the policy for now and schedules a review.

choices.text: Yes, move him; the policy says so, and that is the end of it.
choices.feedback: Following the policy is right, but staff may now think the problem is solved. The message that matters is that technique, not the machine, stops transmission.
choices.then: At the staff huddle you add that hand hygiene audits continue for every station.

n5.scene: The confirmation is positive. No other new positive has appeared so far.
n5.prompt: What do you do next for Mr. Villanueva and the unit?

choices.text: Tell Mr. Villanueva and arrange his hepatitis C evaluation, but keep the investigation inside the unit.
choices.feedback: He needs his result and his care, but a probable unit-acquired infection is also reported per DOH and facility rules. Reporting is part of fixing the system.
choices.then: The infection control nurse files the report with you.

vitals.report: Patient told; reported per DOH and facility rules

choices.text: Wait to tell him until the source is known, so you can give him a full answer.
choices.feedback: His result is his. Delay holds up his own evaluation and erodes trust. You can tell him honestly that the unit is still investigating.
choices.then: The attending asks you to tell him today, together.

vitals.report: Patient told; reported per DOH and facility rules

choices.text: Tell the other patients on his shift which patient has hepatitis C, so they can protect themselves.
choices.feedback: That breaks his confidentiality and protects no one: patients cannot guard themselves against a lapse in staff technique. Exposed patients are tested and informed through infection control, without naming him.
choices.then: The attending stops it. Exposed patients are tested through infection control without being told who the index patient is.

vitals.report: Patient told; reported per DOH and facility rules

choices.text: Tell him honestly with the attending, arrange evaluation, report, keep screening, review the event.
choices.feedback: Honest disclosure, reporting and tracking every result (KDIGO 1B) close the loop. The review turns one patient’s infection into a change in how the whole unit works. Report per DOH and facility rules; keep 6-monthly screening and tracking; test exposed patients as advised; present the event at the unit review.

vitals.report: Patient told; reported per DOH and facility rules

end.title: Six months later
end.text: The next screening round shows no new positive. Monthly hand hygiene observations continue with feedback, medicines are prepared away from the chairs, and the medical director’s policy review has been set against KDIGO 2022 and the DOH licensing rules. Mr. Villanueva is under evaluation for his hepatitis C and still dialyzes on the second shift.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • A new hepatitis C result in a previously negative patient is unit-acquired until shown otherwise. Tell the attending and infection control the same day.
  • Build a line list: all results, stations, shifts, staff, and how medicines and vials are handled.
  • The fix is technique: clean hands at every station, injection safety, cleaning, and observed audits with feedback (KDIGO 1A, 1C).
  • Follow the unit’s licensed policy on machines, and take the KDIGO evidence (1D against dedicated machines) to the medical director.
  • Disclose honestly, protect confidentiality, report, and keep tracking every result.

See Bloodborne viruses and Clusters and outbreaks.
